questions.question: What does a plain `docker run python:3.12 python agent_code.py` take away from the code by default?
options: Very little: it still has network, root inside the container, a writable filesystem and no resource limits
questions.explanation: Container defaults are built for running your own apps, not untrusted code.

questions.question: Why is mounting /var/run/docker.sock into the sandbox critical?
options: The code can ask the root Docker daemon to start a privileged container with the host filesystem mounted
questions.explanation: Access to the Docker API is root on the host.

questions.question: The blog command had 0 critical findings. Why is it still a poor sandbox?
options: It mounts the whole project (.env, .git), runs as root, and has internet and LAN access
questions.explanation: No single flag is catastrophic, but none of the main protections is on.

questions.question: Why does the policy set --memory-swap to the same value as --memory?
options: So the container can't use swap beyond its memory limit
questions.explanation: Equal values mean zero swap, so the memory limit is the real limit.

questions.question: The code needs to pip install packages. What's the better change?
options: Switch to the default bridge network
Attach a network whose only route out is an egress proxy that allows your package index
questions.explanation: Give exactly the access needed, through a point you control and log.

questions.question: Why add gVisor or a microVM on top of a well-configured container for model-written code?
options: Containers share the host kernel, so one kernel bug is an escape; gVisor or a VM puts another kernel boundary in between
questions.explanation: Defence in depth: the code is untrusted, so the boundary should not be a single shared kernel.
